extensions.scope: worker/src/render.ts only. The whole system is one inline STYLE constant in that file. The CLI's terminal table is deliberately undocumented.

paper.purpose: The page behind everything, and the colour showing through the gap between frames.

ink.purpose: The single text colour inside a frame, the wordmark, the tally counts, the section rule.

silver.purpose: The tier that exists only outside a frame, where the ground is always the paper: edge strip, tally labels, age note, captions, commit log, list dashes.

wax.purpose: The only saturated ink on the page. Condition and nothing else: the suspect strike, the suspect count, a stale exposure stamp, the focus ring, the selection highlight.
wax.measured: Light value is measured, not chosen: the strike is a non-text mark needing 3:1 against any ramp step. Clears 3.2:1 on d5 and 6.3:1 on the paper. The previous #c62f22 reached only 2.49:1 on d5.

rebate.purpose: The 1px hairline: edge strip underline, block rules, the inset outline on an unexposed frame and on panels, the underline under a frame name, the fill behind inline code.

density-ramp.purpose: A frame's ground, set by days since its last commit: d0 under 1d, d1 under 3d, d2 under 7d, d3 under 30d, d4 under 90d, d5 beyond. Fixed steps, never computed from the current board. A frame with no git prints as dx: transparent paper with a rebate outline.

display.purpose: The snapshot's age, and nothing else, on any surface. The largest element on every page by a wide margin.

count.purpose: The one line stating how many frames are lying to you. An order of magnitude below the stamp.

headline.purpose: The two section labels, full ink over an ink rule.

title.purpose: A project name in the device's UI face. 1.4rem on a project's own page.

body.purpose: Notes, next items, panel prose. The UI face, because a human wrote it.

label.purpose: Edge strip, tally, back link, project-page block rules. Machine type as measurement.

meta.purpose: Frame head (number, stage), metadata line, git line.

micro.purpose: The next label and the stated-cap line.

mono.purpose: The recent-commit sequence. .78rem on a project page.

shadows.name: rebate-outline
shadows.purpose: The only box-shadow in the system, used twice: an unexposed (dx) frame and the empty / mismatch / missing panel. It is a hairline border drawn inside the box, never elevation. Dark: inset 0 0 0 1px #2a313b.

motion.name: develop
motion.purpose: The only animation in the system. Frames rise to their density once, staggered down the sheet, from an already-visible default (@keyframes develop { from { background-color: var(--paper); } }). Only the ground moves, so every word is readable from the first frame. Wrapped in @media (prefers-reduced-motion: no-preference).

breakpoints.name: two-up
breakpoints.purpose: The sheet goes to 2 columns; the lead section stays at 1. Below the narrowest phone still shipping, so every phone gets two columns.

breakpoints.name: desk
breakpoints.purpose: 3 columns (lead 2), wider body padding, and the lead frames' depth cap is lifted; the +N more line is hidden.

breakpoints.name: wide
breakpoints.purpose: 4 columns (lead 3), body capped at 86rem and centred.

narrative.overview:
This is a darkroom contact sheet: the whole roll printed on one sheet, read at arm's length, with the frames that are lying to you crossed out in grease pencil. A contact sheet exists to answer one question, "what have I actually got", from a single object rather than from a list, and it is honest by construction that it is a print of a moment rather than the negatives. That last part is the product's own confession about staleness, which is why the world fits.

The sheet's tone does the work before any word is read. Every frame prints at a ground set by how long it has been since that project's last commit, on a fixed six-step density ramp, so the sheet's overall shade is the board's shape. The sheet is then cut in two: working on leads, the rest follows, and the cut is the page's main hierarchy. One saturated ink exists on the page, a grease-pencil wax, and it carries condition and nothing else. Everything else is paper, ink, silver and rebate.

Both schemes are first-class and the file carries two full palettes. The light scheme is a print on the bench; the dark scheme is the same sheet on a light table, where the dense frames are the ones that glow. Density still means distance from the ground in both, so the sheet's shape reads identically either way. The dark scheme is the common case: a phone, in the dark, for about four seconds. The world's earlier warm rendition (cream paper, sepia, beige) was built and rejected on 2026-11-02; a darkroom is not a beige place, and the shipped rendition is the cold end of the same room.
keyCharacteristics: Ground tone encodes recency on a fixed six-step ramp; it is never computed from the board.
One saturated ink (wax), reserved for condition. Everything else is a grey.
Square corners everywhere. No radius anywhere in the system.
The rebate is the gap: the page shows through between frames and nothing draws a divider.
Exactly one text colour inside a frame, at full ink.
Machine type (monospace) for everything the machine stamped; the UI face for human text.
One motion in the whole system, and it is the sheet coming up in the developer.

rules.name: The One Ink Rule
rules.body: There is exactly one saturated colour in the system and it reports a condition the data actually holds. It is never used for emphasis, branding, a heading, a link, or because a region looked flat. On a board with nothing suspect and a fresh snapshot, the page is entirely grey, and that is correct.

rules.name: The Density Is Recency Rule
rules.body: A frame's ground is a fixed function of its last commit, on a ramp of six constant steps. It is never a gradient computed across the current board, or the same project would print differently on a different day, and the sheet would stop being comparable with itself. Density is also never used to mean anything else: not stage, not priority, not suspicion.

rules.name: The One Text Colour Inside A Frame Rule
rules.body: Text on a density ground is full ink, always, and the six grounds all clear WCAG 2.2 AA against it. A muted grey tier was tried inside frames on 2026-11-02 and removed the same day: a second text colour has to clear all six steps, a grey that does is no longer muted, and it failed AA at the dense end in both schemes. The silver tier survives only outside the frames. Do not reintroduce a muted colour inside a frame without re-checking it against d5.

rules.name: The No Condition By Colour Alone Rule
rules.body: Every condition ships on at least two channels, and the words are the first one. The suspect state has three: the struck stage, the struck frame number, and the literal ! among the flags, with the wax only agreeing. The exposure stamp's tone is never rendered without its plain-language note. PRODUCT.md holds this page to WCAG 2.2 AA and these states are the entire value of the page.

rules.name: The Stamp Outranks Everything Rule
rules.body: The snapshot age is set larger than the wordmark and larger than every project name, on every surface that exists, including a single project's page. A reader who takes one fact away must take this one, because a dashboard that silently shows yesterday is the exact failure this product exists to prevent. Never let another element outgrow it, and never render a surface without it.

rules.name: The Hierarchy Without A Second Colour Rule
rules.body: Inside a frame, rank is carried by size, weight and tracking only. If something needs to recede, make it smaller or lighter, never greyer.

rules.name: The Monospace Means Machine Rule
rules.body: Monospace marks what the machine stamped or the reader must type: ages, frame numbers, stages, flags, branch names, counts, commands. A project name and a note are human writing and stay in the UI face even though a terminal would set them in mono.

rules.name: The Column Flow Rule
rules.body: The sheet flows down each column, never across rows, at every width. The payload's order is a ranking and the layout must not scramble it. Multicolumn also commits to no row count, which is why it survives from 22rem to 86rem without a second layout.

rules.name: The Cut Rule
rules.body: The sheet is cut into exactly two sections, and the cut is the page's main hierarchy: what you are inside leads, everything else follows. Both sections keep payload order internally, and frame numbers are assigned before the split, so a frame number always means the same rank it means in the terminal and moving a project between sections never renumbers it. The section label is machine type at full ink over an ink rule with air above it: it was silver at .7rem over a rebate rule until 2026-11-02, which is the edge strip's own treatment, and made the second section read as the sheet continuing rather than as a second sheet.

rules.name: The Stated Cap Rule
rules.body: A phone caps a lead frame's depth at two next items and two commits, because six lead frames at four and four put roughly 3000px between the stamp and the rest. The cap is stated by a +2 next line, never silent: a block that quietly drops two of its four items is indistinguishable from a project that only had two. Nothing is capped at 48rem and above, and the line is hidden there.

rules.name: The Density Is Not Elevation Rule
rules.body: A denser frame is older, not nearer. Depth must never become a second channel for condition, and a suspect frame is never raised, outlined or shadowed; it is struck.

rules.name: The Rebate Is The Divider Rule
rules.body: Separation is the gap, not a line. No frame draws a border. The only rules on the page are the edge strip's hairline, the two section rules, and the project page's block rules.

rules.name: The Hand Mark Rule
rules.body: Any mark that represents a human judgement is drawn, slightly off-axis, and overhangs what it marks. Any mark that represents a machine value is square, aligned and tabular. Do not let the two swap.

rules.name: The No Radius Rule
rules.body: Nothing in this system is rounded. A rounded corner is a card, and a card is the vertical stack of status panels this page was redesigned to stop being.

dos: Do keep the exposure stamp the largest element on every surface, larger than the wordmark and every project name, and never render a surface without it.
Do keep text inside a frame at full ink, and build hierarchy from size, weight and tracking.
Do keep silver for what sits on the paper: edge strip, tally, captions, logs, notes.
Do re-check both the wax and the single text ink against d5 in both schemes if any ramp step moves.
Do give every condition a word. Colour agrees with the words; it never carries them alone.
Do flow the sheet down its columns, at every width.
Do state any cap you apply, the way the +2 next line does.
Do use the CLI's exact flag strings so the terminal and the sheet never disagree.
Do keep the whole system inline in render.ts: no framework, no build step, no client fetch, no external font. The page must work with nothing but the HTML that arrives.
Do design dark as its own print. It is the common case, not an inversion.
donts: Don't introduce a second saturated colour, or use wax for anything that is not a condition the data holds.
Don't put wax text on a density ground. Wax stays where its ground is known: the strike, the focus ring, and the stamp block on the paper.
Don't add a muted text tier inside a frame.
Don't compute the density ramp from the current board, or reuse density to mean anything other than recency.
Don't add a drop or offset shadow. The only box-shadow permitted is the 1px inset rebate hairline.
Don't draw a border around a frame. The gap is the divider.
Don't mark a suspect frame with a ring, a tint, or elevation. It is struck.
Don't add a second motion, or let motion start from an invisible state.
Don't re-sort the payload, re-number frames after the section split, or make anything interactive beyond the project link. The dashboard is read-only by product decision.
Don't interpolate a value into the markup without escapeHtml. The rule lives as a comment at that function.
